150 - Black Sabbath and Philosophy - Mas: Black Sabbath, formed in postwar industrial Birmingham in 1968, are widely credited with inventing heavy metal: slow, downtuned riffs, occult imagery, and Ozzy Osbourne's wail over songs about war, paranoia, and the end of the world. Accused of Satanism in their early years, they more plausibly wrote about real horrors, from nuclear annihilation to heroin. This book asks what actually makes their sound feel evil, whether their lyrics amount to an accidental philosophy of despair, and how Nietzsche, Camus, and Schopenhauer illuminate the doom they put on record.
152 - The Ultimate Daily Show and Philos: The Daily Show, Jon Stewart's fake news program on Comedy Central from 1999 to 2015, became an unlikely source of political seriousness for a generation that got its news from comedy. By playing actual news footage straight and then puncturing it, the show forced questions about what television journalism had itself become. The essays here ask how a self-described fake newscast can inform viewers, whether mockery is a legitimate political voice, and what Baudrillard and Postman make of a media world where simulation and reporting blur.
153 - Disney and Philosophy - Truth, Tru: Disney is less a single film than a universe: ninety years of animated classics, Pixar, theme parks, and the modern princess. This book treats that universe as a shared cultural vocabulary worth taking seriously. The essays range from Ariel's traded voice and the male gaze, through Mulan colliding with Confucian ideas of the self, to whether Hidden Mickeys hidden in the parks say anything about God, whether Inside Out gets emotions right, and whether the studio's happy endings are wisdom or calibrated escapism.
154 - Doctor Strange and Philosophy - Th: Doctor Strange began as a 1963 Stan Lee and Steve Ditko comic about an arrogant surgeon turned sorcerer, and reached a mass audience with the 2016 film starring Benedict Cumberbatch. His story, a scientist forced by catastrophe to accept magic, is a natural bridge between two ways of seeing the world. The essays read his crash and convalescence through Nietzsche and Heidegger, his famous 'I've come to bargain' time loop as the eternal return weaponized, and his comic-book trials as a working-out of Descartes' Meditations.
155 - Downton Abbey and Philosophy - The: Downton Abbey, the ITV drama that ran from 2010 to 2015, follows an aristocratic family and their servants through the decline of the English country house in the early twentieth century. Its quiet domestic plots turn out to be dense with moral and social philosophy. The essays ask what makes work meaningful when nobody chooses their station, whether manners are ethics or their disguise, how money corrupts Matthew Crawley's romance, and why viewers raised on equality find the upstairs-downstairs hierarchy so fascinating.
156 - Dune and Philosophy - Minds, Monad: Frank Herbert's Dune, published in 1965, is the best-selling science fiction novel of all time: a desert-planet epic of prophecy, ecology, and a chosen leader whose victory sets off a galactic holy war. Herbert's warning against heroes gives the book unusual philosophical depth. The essays take on Paul's paradoxical foreknowledge, the Bene Gesserit's eugenics programs, Leto II's tyrannical Golden Path, whether the Fremen are quintessentially American, and what Clausewitz and Habermas would make of the jihad Paul could not stop.
157 - Dungeons and Dragons and Philosoph: Dungeons and Dragons, the tabletop role-playing game Gary Gygax and Dave Arneson published in 1974, lets a group of friends build stories together around dice, rules, and improvised characters. Its forty-year lifespan has made it the standard case for what a game can be. The essays ask whether dungeon-crawling is mere escapism or Aristotelian art, whether playing an evil character teaches virtue or corrodes it, how the alignment system maps onto Kant and Mill, and whether grief over a character's death is rational.
158 - Ender's Game and Philosophy - The: Orson Scott Card's 1985 novel Ender's Game follows a gifted child trained through increasingly brutal war games to command humanity's fleet against an alien enemy, only to learn the final game was real. It is a staple of both military reading lists and school curricula, and its premise raises hard questions on purpose. The essays examine Battle School as Plato's Republic, Foucault's Panopticon, and a Freirean nightmare; ask whether Ender is responsible for xenocide he was tricked into; and trace how empathy becomes a weapon.
159 - The Expanse and Philosophy - So Fa: The Expanse, a novel series by James S. A. Corey adapted into a television run from 2015 to 2022, is hard science fiction about a colonized solar system split between Earth, Mars, and the exploited Belters of the asteroid belt, all destabilized by an alien technology. It is prized for taking politics, class, and physics seriously. The essays weigh who is more evil, Amos or Avasarala, whether humanity should risk extinction opening the Ring gates, and what Pascal and Kant make of its terrifying, beautiful infinite space.
160 - Fallout and Philosophy - Thinking: Fallout is a long-running video game series, begun in 1997, set in an America devastated by nuclear war and steeped in 1950s retro-futurism, where players roam the wasteland making faction-defining moral choices. Its vault experiments and mutant underclass are designed as ethical sandboxes. The essays ask whether a wasted world is too cruel to bring children into, whether ghouls, super mutants, and synthetic people count as persons, whether a 'Kill Everything' playthrough corrupts character, and whether the Pip-Boy is literally part of your mind.
